IThe Arrival

The Front Elevation

A Georgian sentence in brick.
The house announces itself by restraint.

200 Hollycrest Drive · 1916

The gate has been open since 1916.

In 1916, those were saplings. Now they are a forest.

Brick massing, balanced windows, a centered entry, white trim. Wings that hold the long Georgian line.

The Threshold · 1916

The house gives you its name
before it gives you a room.

GARRAN HILL · 1916 — inlaid in the threshold brick.

The brass key plates on every door still have their original keys. The door has been open since 1916.

IIThe Page Provenance

Walter Hines Page · 1855–1918

The Vision of Walter Hines Page

Appointed by Wilson.
He held the alliance from London.

Garran Hill begins with Walter Hines Page — editor, author, co-founder of Doubleday, Page & Company, and United States Ambassador to Great Britain during the First World War.

From London, he commissioned a Moore County country estate. He named it Garran Hill. He never spent a night here.

"Build the farm, therefore; and let me hear at every stage of that happy game."Walter Hines Page · Letter from London · 1915
"The friend of Britain in her sorest need."Westminster Abbey · Inscribed 1921
"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?"Aberdeen station · December 1918
IIIThe Rooms

The Staircase

The same curve since 1916.

The mahogany volute turns from the foyer in a single continuous arc — black railing, wooden treads, the wallpaper rising beside it.

It has not been replaced. It has not been rebuilt. It has been climbed every day since the craftsmen who built Pinehurst finished it in 1916.

The Drawing Room

Coffered ceiling. French doors.
They made it bigger so they could dance.

The room runs nearly forty feet, with tall windows down both sides and a fireplace anchoring one end. Coffered ceiling. Georgian molding. Oak floors original to 1916.

French doors open to the south terrace. Room enough to dance.

The Sitting Room

Delft tile. Spiral stair.
Fire going. No one home yet.

Georgian carved mantel. Original Delft tile surround — blue and white, hand-painted. Lion andirons.

A spiral staircase rises from this room to the office above. Seven fireplaces. This one is the one that matters.

The Dining Room

The original frontispiece.
A disappearing folding screen that still works.

Seventeen by nineteen feet. Shell cabinets flanking the fireplace are original to the house.

The folding screen folds flat and disappears into the wall. It has been doing that since 1916.

The Library

Not original.
That is the point.

Three walls. Floor to ceiling. The ladder is still there.

Walter Hines Page was an editor and publisher. He co-founded Doubleday, Page & Company. He edited The Atlantic Monthly. This is the room the house was built around.

The Kitchen

The kitchen is not original to 1916.
It is original to the restoration.

Heart-pine floors. White cabinetry. Dark granite island. Four windows facing the grounds.

The kitchen was not updated. It was designed. The architectural plans — all 15 sheets — transfer with the property.

The Butler's Pantry

Farmhouse sink. Glass-front cabinetry. Patterned wallpaper.

The passage between kitchen and dining room — a service corridor that refused to abandon form.

The Powder Room

A room this small should not work this hard.
It does.

Gilded fixtures. Ornate floral wallpaper. Pedestal basin.

The Primary Suite

A room that faces the grounds on two sides.

The fireplace is centered, flanked by two armchairs. Soft natural light. The palette is quiet.

Mornings here face the trees. Every window faces green.

The Mirror Bath

Gold chandelier.
Not a bathroom. A decision.

Mirrors multiply the light. The fixtures are deliberate. The tile work is precise.

This is the bath that stops you — not because it is large, but because every surface was considered.

IVThe Grounds

4.15 acres.
The house is only the beginning.

The Pool · Salt Water · 20×40
The Wee Cottage
The Grounds

Through old iron gates, the 20×40 in-ground pool catches afternoon light inside its brick walls. Converted to saltwater in 2022.

The Wee Cottage sits tucked behind a wall of azaleas. Its own entrance, its own scale, its own quality of light.

Someone still puts flowers there.
